note: Jurisprudence, Public International Law and Professional Ethics. Principles only; no case is cited and no rule text is quoted. See docs/STYLE.md, 'Never invent a citation'.

cards.back: What law is from what law ought to be. Validity depends on source; justice is a different question and does not decide validity.

cards.front: What does the natural law tradition deny?
cards.back: The separation. On this view law has a moral point, and a rule that betrays it badly enough forfeits its claim to be law.
cards.source: Standard statement of the natural law tradition.

cards.front: Why is positivism said to make criticism of law easier?
cards.back: Because you can say a rule is law and unjust at once. Denying it is law would be needed on the rival view, which muddles the criticism.

cards.front: What is the standard objection to letting injustice defeat validity?
cards.back: Someone must decide when a rule is unjust enough. That hands judges a large power and costs certainty about what the law is.
cards.source: Standard objection to natural law positions.

cards.front: A judge strains a clear statute to avoid an unjust result. Which way does that lean?
cards.back: Towards natural law in effect, whatever it is called — the moral quality of the outcome is shaping what the law is taken to say.

cards.front: Name three practical questions where the positivism debate surfaces.
cards.back: How far a court may strain harsh words; whether a correctly passed amendment can be struck down; what an official should do when a rule is clear and wrong.

cards.front: Malaysia ratifies a treaty. What changes in domestic law?
cards.back: Nothing by itself. Malaysia is dualist: the treaty binds the state internationally, but domestic effect needs legislation.

cards.front: What is the difference between monism and dualism?
cards.back: Monism treats a ratified treaty as part of national law. Dualism treats the systems as separate, so legislation is the bridge.

cards.front: Can an unincorporated treaty affect how a statute is read?
cards.back: Yes, where the statute is ambiguous a court may prefer the reading that fits the state's obligations. It cannot displace clear words.

cards.front: What are the two elements of customary international law?
cards.back: State practice, and a sense of legal obligation. Habit alone is not law and belief alone is not practice.

cards.front: A client's treaty right has not been legislated. What do you check first?
cards.back: Whether an existing statute is ambiguous in a way the treaty could resolve. It is the one route needing no new legislation.

cards.front: Is an unincorporated treaty legally meaningless?
cards.back: No. It binds the state internationally, guides interpretation of ambiguous statutes, and usually shapes the Act that follows.

cards.front: When the client's instructions conflict with the duty to the court, which wins?
cards.back: The duty to the court. It is paramount. The advocate may have to withdraw, but may never deceive.
cards.source: Standard statement of the paramount duty.

cards.front: You find binding authority against your own argument. What must you do?
cards.back: Draw it to the court's attention, then argue why it should not decide this case. Concealing it misleads the court.
cards.source: Standard duty of candour to the court.

cards.front: A client instructs you to run a story you know is false. What is the resolution?
cards.back: Refusal and silence. Refuse to assert it, withdraw if you must, and do not tell the court why — confidence still binds.
cards.source: Interaction of the paramount duty and confidentiality.

cards.front: When does a duty of confidence to a client end?
cards.back: It does not end with the retainer. It survives the case and ordinarily survives the client.
cards.source: Standard statement of the duty of confidence.

cards.front: Name the three kinds of conflict an advocate must check for.
cards.back: Between two clients in the same matter; between client and the advocate's own interest; and from information held from a former client.

cards.front: Under which statute is the legal profession regulated in Malaysia?
cards.back: The Legal Profession Act 1976. Read the professional conduct rules made under it for the binding formulation of these duties.
